title: Iterative life cycles
blurb: Name the iterative phases in order, explain how time boxes, MoSCoW and feedback work, and know when iterative is the right choice.
question: A housing association is building an online portal for tenants. Nobody is sure which features tenants will actually use, and the board wants something live within three months. The project manager proposes short, fixed time boxes with tenant feedback after each. What life cycle is this, what are its phases, and why does it suit this project?

teach.h: Build a little, learn, adjust, repeat
teach.body: An iterative life cycle develops the solution through repeated, time-boxed iterations, with users reviewing each one so their feedback shapes the next. It is based on agile practice (the APM model follows DSDM). Its phases are Feasibility, Foundations, Evolutionary development and Deployment, framed by pre-project and post-project work. In plain English: check it's viable, agree the essentials, then build and release in short cycles, learning as you go.

steps.label: Pre-project
steps.sub: Idea framed and aligned with strategy

steps.label: Feasibility
steps.sub: Is it technically and commercially viable?

steps.label: Foundations
steps.sub: High-level needs, MoSCoW priorities, time-box plan

steps.label:
Evolutionary
development
steps.sub: Repeated time boxes: build, review, refine

steps.label: Post-project
steps.sub: Check the benefits are being realised

teach.caption: Evolutionary development and Deployment can repeat: release an increment, then develop the next.
Each time box ends on its date, finished or not. What was learned reshapes the priorities for the next one.

teach.h: Time and cost fixed, scope flexes
teach.body: A linear project fixes scope and lets time and cost move through change control. Iterative flips this: time and cost are fixed, and scope is what flexes. Requirements are prioritised with MoSCoW (Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have this time). If a time box runs short, lower-priority items are dropped or deferred; the date does not move and quality is not sacrificed. Value is delivered incrementally, so the most important features reach users first.

rows.label: Requirements are uncertain or likely to change
The business needs early value or fast feedback
Users or a product owner can engage throughout
A regulator must approve a complete design first
Late change would mean tearing out physical work

teach.note: Typical homes: software, digital services, research and development, new products.

teach.body: Feasibility: can the portal link to the repairs and rent systems, and will it save call-centre time? Foundations: tenants and staff agree the Must haves (report a repair, pay rent) and six two-week time boxes are planned. Evolutionary development: each time box builds features, a tenant panel tries them, and the product owner reorders the backlog. Deployment: repair reporting goes live after month two, rent payments later. Tenants benefit long before every feature exists.

teach.caption: Deployment is the only shared name: third phase in linear, fourth in iterative.

teach.text: The classic exam trap is mixing linear names into the iterative list. Concept, Definition and Transition are LINEAR. The iterative order is Feasibility, Foundations, Evolutionary development, Deployment. A second trap: iterative does not mean 'no planning' or 'no governance'. Foundations plans the time boxes, and every time box is reviewed; governance is lighter and more frequent, not absent.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the phases in order: Feasibility, Foundations, Evolutionary development, Deployment.
Explain time boxes: fixed time and cost, scope flexing by MoSCoW priority, quality protected.
Explain the feedback loop: users review each increment, so requirements are refined as you go.
Say when it fits: uncertain or evolving requirements, need for early value, engaged users.
Note what it needs: a committed product owner and discipline to stop scope drifting.
Iterative phases in order: Feasibility, Foundations, Evolutionary development, Deployment.
Work happens in fixed time boxes; feedback after each reshapes the next.
Time and cost are fixed; scope flexes using MoSCoW; quality is protected.
Value is released in increments, long before the whole solution is finished.
Concept, Definition and Transition are linear names, never iterative.

summary: You can now name the iterative phases in order and explain how time boxes, MoSCoW prioritisation and user feedback work together. You can also judge when an iterative life cycle is applicable and spot a linear phase name hiding in an iterative list.

A.q: Which is the correct order of the phases in an iterative life cycle?
A.why: The iterative order is Feasibility, Foundations, Evolutionary development, Deployment.

whyNot.0: Feasibility comes first: you check viability before laying the foundations.
whyNot.2: Transition is a LINEAR phase; the iterative life cycle ends in Deployment.
whyNot.3: Concept is the first LINEAR phase; the iterative model starts with Feasibility.

A.q: On an iterative project the time box is running short. Which element normally gives way?
A.why: Time and cost are fixed and quality is protected, so lower-priority scope is dropped or deferred.

whyNot.0: Time boxes have fixed end dates; moving them undermines the approach.
whyNot.1: Cost is fixed per time box; the budget does not simply grow.
whyNot.2: Quality is protected; cutting it would deliver features that don't work.

options: A fixed period with a fixed end date
A phase that ends at a decision gate
A store for the project's documents
A buffer added at the end of a plan
A.why: A time box is a fixed period of time, with a fixed end date, in which a prioritised set of work is attempted.

whyNot.1: Phases ending in decision gates describe the linear life cycle.
whyNot.2: Document storage is information management, not a time box.
whyNot.3: A buffer at the end of a schedule is a critical chain idea, not a time box.

B.q: Which situation most strongly suggests an iterative life cycle?
options: A regulator must approve a fixed design
Late changes would mean demolishing work
Users cannot yet say what they need
The full scope is specified in a contract
B.why: When users cannot yet define their needs, building in increments and learning from their feedback is the safest route.

whyNot.0: A fixed design approved up front suits a linear approach.
whyNot.1: Costly late change is a reason to plan fully first, which is linear.
whyNot.3: A fully specified scope removes the main reason for iterating.

B.q: Who on an iterative project owns and prioritises the backlog and accepts the work each iteration?
B.why: The product owner represents the business, owns and prioritises the backlog and accepts completed work each iteration.

whyNot.1: The sponsor owns the business case and is accountable for benefits, but doesn't manage the backlog day to day.
whyNot.2: A PMO supports with standards and reporting; it doesn't own the product's priorities.
whyNot.3: A senior supplier represents those delivering the work, not the business priorities.

B.q: Which is NOT a distinctive feature of an iterative life cycle?
options: A scope fixed at the outset
B.why: A scope fixed at the outset is a linear feature. In iterative working the scope flexes within fixed time and cost.

whyNot.0: Incremental delivery is central to iterative working.
whyNot.1: Feedback after every time box is what makes it iterative.
whyNot.3: MoSCoW is how iterative projects decide what flexes.

C.q: Halfway through a time box, Hearthside's team realises not every planned feature will be finished. What should normally happen?
options: Extend the time box by a week
Cut testing to finish on time
C.why: The time box date and cost hold, and quality is protected, so the lowest-priority (Could have) items are deferred.

whyNot.0: Extending the time box breaks the fixed-time principle.
whyNot.2: Cutting testing sacrifices quality, which iterative working protects.
whyNot.3: Cost is fixed, so adding budget is not the normal response.

C.q: A council's digital team releases a first usable version after six weeks and adds features every fortnight. What is the main benefit to the council?
options: The total cost is known on day one
No more user input will be needed
C.why: Incremental releases put useful features into service early, so value starts before the whole solution is complete.

whyNot.0: Iterative fixes cost per time box, but the final total scope is harder to forecast.
whyNot.1: Iterative working depends on continuing user input.
whyNot.2: Most scope change is handled through the backlog, but changes to fixed time, cost or objectives still need control.

C.q:
Which TWO conditions matter most for an iterative life cycle to succeed?
1) Engaged users or an available product owner
2) A detailed specification signed off before build
3) Willingness to let scope flex
4) A single handover at the very end
C.why: Iterative working needs people available to give feedback and decide priorities, and acceptance that scope will flex.

whyNot.0: A full signed-off specification before build is a linear condition.
whyNot.2: Both are linear features: an up-front specification and a single final handover.
whyNot.3: Willingness to flex is right, but a single final handover contradicts incremental delivery.

reteach.title: Developing a new restaurant menu
reteach.question: A chef opening a new restaurant isn't sure which dishes diners will love. Rather than fixing a full menu, she runs tasting nights and adjusts. How does that match the iterative phases?

blocks.body: Feasibility: could this restaurant work here, and would it pay? Foundations: the must-have dishes, the kitchen rules and a plan of weekly tasting nights. Evolutionary development: each week is a time box: the night is fixed, the dishes change based on diners' comments. Deployment: winning dishes go onto the real menu, week by week. The opening date never moves; the menu does.

blocks.loop: Next tasting night: refine and repeat

steps.label: Deployment
steps.sub: Proven dishes go on the menu

blocks.text: Notice what never appears: no Concept, no Definition, no Transition. Those three belong to the linear model.

explain.body: Feasibility checks whether the idea is technically and commercially viable. Foundations then lays the groundwork: high-level requirements prioritised with MoSCoW, the approach, and a plan of time boxes. Detail is left to emerge later.

test.q: An iterative project has just confirmed it is technically and commercially viable. Which phase comes next?
test.why: After Feasibility comes Foundations, where high-level requirements are prioritised and the time boxes are planned.

whyNot.2: Deployment comes after development has produced something to release.
whyNot.3: Development starts only once the foundations are in place.

explain.body: The heart of the model: repeated time boxes. Each builds part of the solution, demonstrates it to users and gathers feedback, which reorders the backlog. Risks and requirements are revisited every time box rather than once at the start.

test.q: What is the main role of user feedback during evolutionary development?
options: To fix the scope for good
test.why: Feedback on each increment validates what has been built and refines the requirements for the next time box.

whyNot.0: Iterative scope keeps evolving; feedback does not freeze it.
whyNot.1: Phase-end gates are a linear governance feature.
whyNot.3: Feedback complements testing; quality is still checked.

explain.h: Fixed time and cost, flexible scope
explain.body: Iterative projects hold the time box date and the cost, protect quality, and flex the scope. MoSCoW decides what gives way: Could haves first, then Should haves. Must haves are the minimum that must be delivered.

test.q: If a time box overruns, which MoSCoW category is normally the first to be dropped?
test.why: Could haves are the lowest-priority items in scope, so they are the first to be deferred when time is short.

whyNot.0: Must haves are the minimum usable solution; they are protected.
whyNot.1: Should haves are important and only dropped after Could haves.
whyNot.2: Won't haves were never in this time box's scope.

explain.body: Choose iterative when requirements are uncertain or evolving, when the business needs value or feedback early, and when users or a product owner can stay engaged. It is common in software, digital services and research and development.

test.q: A pharmaceutical start-up is exploring a new lab-testing tool. Its scientists will refine what they need as they try early versions. Which life cycle fits best?
test.why: Requirements will emerge as scientists try early versions, which is exactly what iterative feedback loops are designed for.

whyNot.1: Linear needs stable requirements up front, which the scientists can't yet give.
whyNot.2: An extended life cycle adds benefits phases; it doesn't answer how to handle uncertain requirements.
whyNot.3: A strictly sequential approach is linear and would freeze requirements too early.
